title: Atomic Structure Determination of Amorphous Solids
content: Electron microscopy images at best are two-dimensional projections of three-dimensional objects under optimal imaging and sample conditions. The loss of information from the projection process, coupled with experimental noise, limits the information content. This difficulty, which is well-known, presents a significant challenge for atomic structure determination of amorphous solids. Unlike crystals where the periodicity limits the number of atoms whose position needs to be determined, every atom in an amorphous solid is uniquely different from others, and the structure determination thus requires the identification of each atom position and chemical identity. Alternatively, diffraction patterns recorded from amorphous samples can be analyzed for the determination of pair distribution function (PDF) using X-ray and neutron diffraction [1] and for fluctuation analysis using electrons [2,3,4]. These quantities describe the probability of finding neighboring-atoms at a distance and deviations from such statistics in the form of medium range order. However, diffraction-based analysis requires the support of theoretical models to gain insights about the atomic structure, and it is not clear whether the model interpretation can be unique.
